title: Implement interpolated LUT application to L* channel
description: Add `apply_lut` to `src/lumamatch/tonemap.py`, mapping a per-pixel L* array through the bin-resolution LUT with linear interpolation. Interpolation rather than bin snapping is required: snapping would quantize every pixel to one of `bins` discrete L* values and produce visible banding in smooth gradients.
acceptanceCriteria: `apply_lut(l_star, lut, edges) -> np.ndarray` returns float64 of the same shape as `l_star`
Output is monotonic in the input: sorting the input and mapping yields a non-decreasing output
Two pixels with equal input L* always produce equal output L*
Input below the first bin center clamps to `lut[0]`; input above the last bin center clamps to `lut[-1]` (no extrapolation past the ends)
A gradient input produces a smooth output with more than `bins` distinct values, demonstrating interpolation rather than snapping
An identity LUT (bin centers) returns the input within one half bin width
Unit tests cover all the above including an explicit banding check; `ruff check` clean

steps.details: Raise `ValueError` if `len(lut) + 1 != len(edges)`. Call the existing `assert_monotonic(lut)` from TASK-11 so a hand-constructed bad LUT cannot be applied silently.

`centers = bin_centers(edges)`. Return `np.interp(l_star, centers, lut)`. Using centers (not edges) as the x-grid is what makes the mapping continuous and correctly aligned with how `build_lut` indexed its output — one LUT value per bin, located at that bin's center.

steps.description: Rely on np.interp's clamping and clip the range
steps.details: np.interp clamps to `lut[0]` and `lut[-1]` outside the xp range by default, which is the desired behavior for the sub-first-center and super-last-center tails. Then apply `np.clip(result, L_MIN, L_MAX)` and ensure the returned dtype is float64 with the input's shape preserved.
np.interp flattens its input. Reshape the result back with `.reshape(l_star.shape)` so an (H,W) L* plane comes back as (H,W). Add a test asserting shape preservation for a (7,11) input.

In `tests/test_tonemap_apply.py`: build a random LUT via `build_lut` on random histograms; apply to `np.sort(random_l_values)` and assert `np.all(np.diff(out) >= 0)`. Separately, apply to an array containing duplicate values and assert the duplicates map to identical outputs.

steps.description: Test that interpolation actually happens (no banding)
steps.details: Build a 1024-sample linear L* ramp from 0 to 100 and a non-trivial LUT with bins=16. Assert `len(np.unique(apply_lut(ramp, lut, edges))) > 16` — proof that the output is not quantized to the 16 LUT values. This is the anti-banding regression test.

steps.description: Test identity, clamping, and error paths
steps.details: Identity: pass `lut = bin_centers(edges)` and assert output is within `bin_width/2` of the input for values inside [centers[0], centers[-1]]. Clamping: assert `apply_lut(np.array([0.0]), ...) == lut[0]` and `apply_lut(np.array([100.0]), ...) == lut[-1]`. Error: mismatched lengths raise ValueError.
Run `.venv/bin/pytest tests/ -q` and `.venv/bin/ruff check src tests`.

technicalNotes: Interpolating against bin CENTERS rather than edges is the subtle correctness point. Using edges would introduce a half-bin shift (about 0.2 L* at 256 bins) that shows up as a small but persistent EMD floor in TASK-21.
Clamping at the ends means the darkest and brightest pixels cannot be pushed beyond lut[0]/lut[-1]. That is intentional and preserves monotonicity; extrapolation could overshoot outside [0,100].
np.interp is O(n log bins) and fully vectorized — no need for a manual searchsorted implementation.
The banding test is the reason this design was chosen over bin snapping; do not weaken it if it fails, fix the interpolation.
